title: Health Canada seizes peptides from Toronto shop, warns of health risks of unregulated market
summary: Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.
Experts warn products being sold are unregulated and untested
Why Health Canada seized 'unauthorized injectable peptides' from Toronto shop
Health Canada has seized a number of injectable peptides from a store in Toronto's Queen West neighbourhood, CBC News has learned.

Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides, on Nov. 9. It also seized bacteriostatic water products, which are often used to reconstitute freeze-dried peptides.

The federal health agency has warned the Canadian public against using unauthorized peptides, which many have purchased online or acquired through compounding pharmacies. The agency said it wasn't able to provide any further detail about its ongoing investigation at Not Peptides, which runs both a bricks-and-mortar and online shop.
"Selling unauthorized health products is illegal," Geneviève Lapierre, a spokesperson for the department, said in an emailed statement.
"Health Canada will continue to seize unauthorized peptide products and disrupt distribution channels to remove these products from the Canadian market."
Not Peptides, which remained open after the seizure, did not respond to CBC Toronto's request for comment.

Peptides are short chains of linked amino acids that serve as the building blocks of proteins, and occur naturally in the body. But the injectable peptides being sold by Not Peptides are largely unproven products that, in many cases, have become popular as fitness influencers claim they can fuel muscle recovery and reverse the signs of aging.

One vial for sale at Not Peptides, a mix of three different peptides including BPC-157, is described on the store's website as being "engineered for synergistic skin renewal, connective-tissue integrity, and accelerated wound closure."
Experts have highlighted there are no large-scale human efficacy trials for BPC-157.

items: Doctors are using a regulatory gap to prescribe an unauthorized peptide

blocks.text: What's behind the peptide boom?
Some peptide-based medications have legitimate medical applications and have been approved for use in Canada.

Experts like David Sabatino, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at Carleton University, have pointed out they can be used properly, highlighting the popularity of peptide-based medications like GLP-1 — often better known under brand names like Ozempic.
But that's fueled interest in other untested peptides, which come with more risk.
“We should take extra caution and be very careful with the risks that are associated with using peptides that have not gone through that approval process,” Sabatino said.

One of his biggest concerns is the potential for contamination in products that have not undergone proper quality control. Sabatino pointed to reports of contaminants, toxins and bacteria in unregulated products, which can lead to infections and other serious complications.

blocks.text: Health Canada warns on its website that taking untested peptides increases the risk of hormonal imbalance, mood swings, blood sugar imbalance, liver or kidney damage, blood clots and even the growth of cancerous tumours.

Public Health Ontario told CBC News it does not systematically collect specific emergency department visit data related to peptide use, making it difficult to determine how many people may be experiencing complications.
City not taking enforcement action against shop
The situation has echoes of Toronto’s early cannabis dispensary crackdown, when stores continued reopening despite repeated police raids. Several of those shops are still operating in Toronto.
The City of Toronto said Not Peptides doesn't have a business licence because of the type of service it provides.
"As a result, no city business licence is required and no licensing enforcement action has been taken," spokesperson Mahreen Dasoo said in an email.
How Canadians are getting unauthorized peptides
Toronto police said in an email its officers weren't involved in Health Canada's seizure.

Health Canada has made similar seizures before, including a wellness shop in Ottawa. Three days before Not Peptides was investigated, Health Canada also issued a public warning after lab testing found bacteria in some peptide products sold by two online retailers.
"Do not buy or use these products," the warning states.
'My first concern if public safety,' physician says
The popularity of peptides, particularly among people seeking cosmetic and performance-related benefits, is growing according to Dr. Jennifer Pearlman.
The Toronto physician who administers peptide therapies says social media influencers have also played a role in promoting these products.
Peptides have already been used in cosmetic products for decades, she says.
When administered safely, and under the supervision of a physician, Pearlman says there are benefits and peptides in the world of medicine hold great promise.
Dr. Jennifer Pearlman is the medical director and CEO of Pearl Rejuvenation in Toronto's Yonge-St. Clair neighbourhood. (Submitted by Jennifer Pearlman)
"They hold enormous therapeutic potential but they are biologically active compounds," she said, adding she was alarmed by what she saw on the shop's website.
"My first concern is public safety. Like all medicines, peptides should be prescribed by a physician to a patient, carefully considering both risk and benefit."
